interviewQuestions.question: A teammate wrote a grouping solution and reported its complexity as "O(n), since it's just a hashmap." When would you push back on that?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd push back whenever the signature computation itself isn't O(1) per item — which is most real grouping problems. The hashmap insert side really is O(n) amortized total, but that's only half the cost; the other half is however expensive it is to *compute* each item's signature, and that cost has to be multiplied across all n items, not waved away.

Concrete case: Group Anagrams isn't O(n) — it's O(n · m log m) for n strings of length m, because sorting each string to build its signature is O(m log m), and that happens n times. Calling it "O(n)" hides the actual dominant cost and would understate the real runtime on long strings even for a modest n.

The general rule I'd apply when reviewing a grouping solution: complexity is **(cost to compute one signature) × n**, plus the O(n) (or O(n log n), if the output itself needs sorting) for the map operations — and both parts need to be named, because either one can dominate depending on the problem. A digit-sum signature is O(digits) per item, essentially O(1) for reasonable inputs, so "O(n)" is actually fair there — but that's a property of *that specific* signature, not a general truth about grouping.

So my pushback wouldn't be "you're wrong," it would be "walk me through what the signature computation costs per item, because that's usually where the real complexity is hiding."

**Testing:** whether you can review someone else's complexity claim critically and separate "the map is fast" from "the whole algorithm is fast," which is exactly where junior complexity analysis tends to go wrong.
